reason: The sources contain nearly 20 cross-verified claims across independent sites regarding Pluto's discovery, orbital characteristics, physical properties, atmosphere, reclassification, and robotic exploration.
story: When Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto at Lowell Observatory in 1930 using a blink comparator, it was celebrated as the Solar System's ninth planet. Named after a suggestion by eleven-year-old Venetia Burney, Pluto soon proved to be a world of contradictions. Smaller than Earth's Moon and seven other solar system moons, Pluto follows an extreme path. Its orbit is tilted over 17 degrees and is so eccentric that it spent 1979 to 1999 closer to the Sun than Neptune. Furthermore, Pluto and its giant moon Charon are mutually tidally locked, endlessly showing each other the same face during their 6.4-day rotation. The discovery of other distant icy bodies, particularly Eris, triggered an astronomical reckoning. In August 2006, the International Astronomical Union formally redefined a planet, requiring a world to clear its orbital neighborhood. Because Pluto shares its realm, it was reclassified as a dwarf planet, a title confirmed when NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew past in July 2015.
angle: Pluto is smaller than Earth's Moon and seven other moons in the Solar System, yet it boasts five moons of its own and an orbit so tilted and elliptical that it was closer to the Sun than Neptune from 1979 to 1999.

claims.claim: Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto at Lowell Observatory in February 1930.
Tombaugh discovered Pluto by using a machine called a blink comparator to inspect pairs of photographic plates.
The name Pluto was first proposed by an 11-year-old English schoolgirl named Venetia Burney.
Pluto's symbol is a monogram combining the letters P and L, which also serve as Percival Lowell's initials.
Pluto's orbit is tilted at an inclination of over 17 degrees relative to the orbital plane of the major planets.
Pluto has an eccentric, elliptical orbit that periodically brings it closer to the Sun than Neptune.
Pluto was closer to the Sun than Neptune between 1979 and 1999.
Pluto is smaller in both size and mass than Earth's Moon.
Seven solar system moons are larger than Pluto: Ganymede, Titan, Callisto, Io, Earth's Moon, Europa, and Triton.
Pluto and its largest moon Charon are tidally locked to each other, permanently facing the same side toward one another.
Pluto's rotation period on its axis takes approximately 6.4 Earth days.
Pluto has a thin, tenuous atmosphere composed primarily of nitrogen.
In August 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) officially redefined the term 'planet' and classified Pluto as a dwarf planet.
The IAU definition requires a planet to orbit the Sun, be massive enough for gravity to pull it into a rounded shape, and clear its orbital neighborhood.
Pluto was designated a dwarf planet because it failed the requirement to clear the neighborhood around its orbit.
The discovery of Eris, a massive trans-Neptunian object, intensified the astronomical debate that led to Pluto's reclassification.
Ceres and Eris were classified as dwarf planets alongside Pluto by the IAU.
NASA's New Horizons spacecraft completed the first flyby of Pluto in July 2015.
Pluto has five known moons: Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra.

disputed: Whether Pluto's name inspired Disney's character Pluto: S1 notes Disney introduced the dog in 1930, but animator Ben Sharpsteen could not confirm the exact reason for the name; scripts should treat this as a cultural coincidence or attribute it.

Comet tail hypothesis: S5 suggests Pluto would grow a tail if moved close to Earth, whereas S1 notes this claim is disputed because Pluto's escape velocity is too high; scripts should leave out the comet tail assertion.

Atmospheric collapse expectations: S1 and S7 note scientists initially expected Pluto's atmosphere to collapse and freeze onto the surface as it moved farther from the Sun, but flyby and occultation data revealed a persistent and dynamic atmosphere; scripts should frame early collapse predictions as past hypotheses.
